title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (Dynamo-style)
prompt: Design a highly available, horizontally scalable distributed key-value store in the style of Amazon Dynamo — one that stays writable during partitions and node failures. Cover partitioning, replication, how reads and writes stay consistent enough, membership, and failure handling.
blurb: The Dynamo playbook: partitioning, quorums, vector clocks, gossip, hinted handoff, and tunable consistency.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (get/put by key, tunable consistency) from non-functional (always-writable, high availability, partition tolerance, scale, durability).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about consistency needs, value size, read/write mix, availability vs consistency priority, conflict tolerance, multi-region.

rubric.label: Estimations
rubric.description: Estimates QPS, dataset size, nodes, replication factor overhead, storage per node.

rubric.label: Partitioning
rubric.description: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes; even distribution; how key ranges map to nodes; add/remove with minimal movement.

rubric.label: Replication
rubric.description: N replicas via preference list on the ring; coordinator; sloppy quorum; cross-node/rack/region placement.

rubric.label: Quorum & tunable consistency
rubric.description: N/R/W quorum math (R+W>N), read-repair, tunable per-request consistency, CAP positioning (AP with eventual consistency).

rubric.label: Conflict resolution
rubric.description: Concurrent writes → vector clocks / version vectors, sibling detection, last-write-wins vs application-level merge, tombstones.

rubric.label: Membership & gossip
rubric.description: Decentralized membership via gossip, failure detection (phi-accrual), no single coordinator, ring propagation.

rubric.label: Failure handling
rubric.description: Hinted handoff for temporary failures, anti-entropy / Merkle trees for permanent divergence, sloppy quorum tradeoffs.

rubric.label: Storage engine
rubric.description: Per-node engine (LSM vs B-tree), write path (commit log + memtable + SSTable), compaction, durability.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Client → coordinator node → preference-list replicas with quorum; read/write path end to end.

rubric.label: Scaling & bottlenecks
rubric.description: Rebalancing, hot partitions, tombstone/compaction load, gossip overhead at large N.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Per-op latency, quorum failures, hinted-handoff/anti-entropy backlog, replica lag, compaction stats.

functional_requirements: get(key) and put(key, value) as the core API
Tunable per-request consistency (choose R and W)
Always accept writes (highly available) even under failures/partitions
Automatic recovery and reconciliation after failures
nonfunctional_requirements: Highly available and partition-tolerant (AP; eventual consistency)
Horizontally scalable to thousands of nodes, incremental growth
No single point of failure — fully decentralized
clarifying_questions: How strong must consistency be — can the app tolerate eventual/conflicting reads?
Is availability strictly prioritized over consistency (Dynamo-style AP)?
Can the application resolve conflicts, or do we need server-side LWW?
qualifying_questions: Do we need range queries/secondary indexes, or pure key access?
What's the durability requirement — how many replicas must ack before we call a write safe?

estimations.traffic: 1M ops/s; with N=3 replication each write touches 3 nodes → ~3M internal write ops/s
estimations.storage: 100TB dataset × N=3 ≈ 300TB raw; ~few TB per node → hundreds of nodes plus headroom
estimations.replication_overhead: N=3 triples storage and write amplification; quorum reads touch R nodes each
estimations.gossip: Gossip is O(nodes) chatter; at thousands of nodes must be bounded/periodic to stay cheap

data_model: Ring: key → hash position → first N distinct nodes clockwise = preference list
value record: {value, version (vector clock), timestamp, tombstone?}
hinted writes: {intended_node, key, value, vclock} buffered on a stand-in node
per-node LSM: commit log + memtable → SSTables + Merkle tree per range for anti-entropy
api_design: put(key, value, context?) with consistency W → { version }
get(key) with consistency R → { value(s), context } (may return siblings to reconcile)
context carries the vector clock the client last saw (for causal writes)
Per-request N/R/W knobs (e.g. W=1 fast+risky, R=W=quorum for R+W>N)
reference.high_level_design: Keys are placed on a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes; the first N distinct physical nodes clockwise from the key's hash form its preference list (spread across racks/regions). Any node can act as coordinator: on put, the coordinator writes locally and forwards to the other replicas, acking once W replicas confirm; on get, it queries the preference list and returns once R respond, performing read-repair on stale replicas. With R+W>N the read and write quorums overlap, giving read-your-writes-style guarantees while staying available. Concurrent writes produce divergent versions tracked by vector clocks — the store detects siblings and either resolves by last-write-wins or returns them for application-level merge, with tombstones for deletes. Membership and liveness propagate via gossip with a phi-accrual failure detector (no central coordinator). Temporary failures are covered by hinted handoff (a healthy node holds writes destined for a down node and replays them on recovery), and permanent divergence is repaired by anti-entropy using Merkle trees to find and sync differing key ranges. Each node stores data in an LSM engine (commit log + memtable + SSTables + compaction).

deep_dives.probe: Walk me through N, R, W. Show me why R+W>N gives overlap, what W=1/R=1 vs quorum buys you, and what 'sloppy quorum' means when the natural replicas are down.

Two clients put the same key concurrently on different coordinators during a partition. Both succeed. What does a later get return, and how do vector clocks let you tell a true conflict from a causal overwrite?
A replica is down for 10 minutes, then for 3 days. Contrast hinted handoff (temporary) with anti-entropy / Merkle-tree repair (permanent divergence) — when does each kick in and what does each cost?
No central coordinator — how do nodes learn the ring and detect failures? Explain gossip and why a phi-accrual detector beats a fixed timeout heartbeat.
How do virtual nodes improve balance and make adding/removing a node cheap? What moves when a node joins, and how do you avoid a rebalancing storm?

Why an LSM tree over a B-tree for this write-heavy store? Walk the write path (commit log → memtable → SSTable), and explain how compaction and tombstones interact — including the deleted-data-resurrection risk.
A read-through cache sits in front of hot keys. When a hot key's cache entry expires and quorum reads flood the replicas, how do you prevent a stampede onto the store?

You want to stream every change out to search/analytics. In an eventually-consistent, multi-version store, how do you do change data capture (CDC/Debezium-style) correctly given siblings, out-of-order writes, and tombstones?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions quorum or consistency or R and W
followup_bank.question: Why does R+W>N matter, and what exactly do you give up choosing W=1 for lower write latency? What's a sloppy quorum?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions vector clock or version or conflict
followup_bank.question: How does a vector clock distinguish a concurrent conflict from a causal overwrite, and who resolves siblings — the store (LWW) or the application?
How is the preference list chosen on the ring, and how do you ensure replicas span racks/regions for fault isolation?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions failure or down node or recovery
followup_bank.question: Hinted handoff vs anti-entropy/Merkle trees — when does each apply, and what's the cost of each during recovery?
Why gossip + phi-accrual failure detection instead of a central coordinator or fixed heartbeat timeouts?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions lsm or storage or compaction
followup_bank.question: Walk the LSM write path and explain how tombstones + compaction can resurrect deleted data if GC grace is mishandled.
For a read-through cache over hot keys, what's the eviction policy and how do you prevent a stampede of quorum reads when a hot key expires?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions cdc or stream or search index
followup_bank.question: How do you do CDC out of an eventually-consistent multi-version store — handling siblings, out-of-order writes, and tombstones without emitting corrupt downstream state?

scaling: Consistent hashing + virtual nodes for even load and cheap incremental scaling
Tunable N/R/W per request to trade latency vs consistency vs durability
Sloppy quorum + hinted handoff to stay available during transient failures
Anti-entropy with Merkle trees to bound reconciliation cost
LSM compaction tuned to control write/space amplification
Bounded, periodic gossip to keep membership overhead sublinear in practice
bottlenecks: Hot partition/key overloading a preference list
Compaction I/O and space amplification under write-heavy load
Anti-entropy / hinted-handoff backlog after long outages
Gossip and coordination overhead as node count grows
Cross-region write latency for wide replication
tradeoffs: AP + eventual consistency (always writable, may read stale/siblings) vs CP (linearizable, may reject during partition)
Low R/W (fast, weaker) vs quorum R+W>N (stronger, higher latency)
LWW conflict resolution (simple, can lose writes) vs vector-clock siblings + app merge (correct, complex)
LSM (write-optimized, compaction cost) vs B-tree (read-optimized, write amplification)
Strict quorum (consistent, may fail writes) vs sloppy quorum (available, temporary inconsistency)
alternative_solutions: CP quorum store (Raft/Paxos per shard, e.g. Spanner/CockroachDB-style) when strong consistency is required
CRDTs for automatic, conflict-free merge instead of vector-clock siblings
Range partitioning (ordered, range scans) instead of hash partitioning (even load, no scans)
observability: Per-op latency and quorum success/failure rates
Hinted-handoff queue depth and anti-entropy repair backlog
Compaction throughput, SSTable counts, tombstone ratios
Gossip convergence time and failure-detector accuracy
security: Authn/authz between clients and nodes and node-to-node (mutual TLS)
Encryption at rest and in transit for replicated data
Isolate/limit tenants to prevent hot-partition noisy-neighbor abuse
reference.reference_answer: A staff-level answer reconstructs the Dynamo design coherently: consistent hashing with virtual nodes for partitioning; an N-node preference list (spread across racks/regions) for replication with any node able to coordinate; and tunable N/R/W quorums where R+W>N gives overlapping read/write sets. It handles concurrent writes with vector clocks — distinguishing causal overwrites from true conflicts (siblings) and choosing LWW vs application-level merge, with tombstones for deletes. It uses decentralized gossip membership with phi-accrual failure detection (no coordinator), covers temporary failures with sloppy quorum + hinted handoff and permanent divergence with anti-entropy Merkle-tree repair, and picks an LSM storage engine (commit log → memtable → SSTable → compaction), including the tombstone/GC-grace resurrection hazard. It positions the system explicitly on CAP (AP, eventual consistency) and names the real bottlenecks — hot partitions, compaction/tombstone load, and reconciliation backlog after outages. Strong candidates also address correct CDC over a multi-version, sibling-bearing store.

interviewer_notes: This is a staff question — expect the candidate to synthesize the whole Dynamo playbook, not just name pieces. The four load-bearing deep dives are quorum math (R+W>N and sloppy quorum), conflict resolution (vector clocks: causal vs concurrent, who merges), failure handling (hinted handoff vs anti-entropy/Merkle trees — when each applies), and decentralized gossip + phi-accrual. Push for precision: many candidates say 'vector clocks' without explaining sibling detection, or 'quorum' without the overlap argument. The LSM storage-engine detail (and the tombstone-resurrection / GC-grace hazard) is a great staff differentiator. Fire the CDC/Debezium probe with the twist that CDC over an eventually-consistent multi-version store is genuinely hard (siblings, reordering, tombstones); fire the cache eviction/stampede probe for hot keys. Have them place the system on CAP explicitly and defend the AP choice. Reserve time for hot partitions and reconciliation backlog as the real operational bottlenecks.
